newsitem.title: UK: Stronger UK PMI, M0 make rate cut hard to justify.
newsitem.headline: Stronger UK PMI, M0 make rate cut hard to justify.

text.p: Signs that Britain's manufacturing industry is on the road to recovery, and stronger-than-expected money supply figures will make it tougher for Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to argue for another rate cut.
But few analysts are prepared to completely rule out a further reduction, possibly at Wednesday's monetary meeting.

"This shows the good news on retail spending we've seen recently is having a beneficial effect on manufacturers," Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International, told Reuters Financial Television.
"It's less easy now for the Chancellor to justify any further interest rate cuts," he added.
The purchasing managers survey for August read 51.8, its highest level in a year. A reading above 50 suggests the manufacturing economy is expanding.
August M0 data, released at the same time, showed narrow money grew at a seasonally adjusted 7.5 percent year-on-year. Economists had forecast growth of 7.0 percent.
Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers, noted that the PMI survey had now produced three consecutive readings above 50, but each only just above.

"The survey shows manufacturing off its knees but it's sluggish," he said, adding that the Chancellor can be confident of not seeing runaway growth in official industrial production figures over the next couple of months.
Dicks said if Clarke did wish to cut base rates again he would have to act soon as the economic data will only strengthen and the U.S. may tighten policy at some point.
"We think there's a 60 percent chance of one last cut and this week's as good a bet as any," he said.
Other analysts said the chances of a monetary easing were receding fast.
"The chances of another rate cut are really falling by the wayside," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

He said PMI survey evidence of rising manufacturing orders and output along with production of intermediate goods, rising sharply as firms restocked warehouses to meet higher demand, all suggested consumer spending was beginning to feed right through the economy.
The PMI prices rose to 41.5 in August from 38.5 in July, but Barr said that had been expected and did not herald inflationary pressures at this stage.
Dicks agreed. He said more worrying for Clarke were the M0 data although the Treasury tends to play down the importance of the narrow money measure.
"M0 has clearly accelerated, miles above the official target," Dicks said. "It's hard to tally 7.5 percent money growth, on a consistent basis, with weak sales."

The government has set a monitoring range for M0 of zero to four percent. Ian Shepherdson, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said Bank of England Governor Eddie George may argue that the renewed strength in M0 points to stronger retail spending.
"We think Mr Clarke will bide his time and leave rates on hold until next month at the earliest," he said.
